resources.string: Palatine tonsils and adenoids both sample material at mucosal surfaces. The cellular close-up follows one palatine crypt, not an adenoid fold. Sizes and timing are schematic.

The pharyngeal tonsil, also called the adenoids, sits high behind the nose. The paired palatine tonsils sit lower, one on each side of the throat behind the mouth. This side view shows the nearer palatine tonsil.

A palatine crypt is a deep pocket lined by the surface tissue. The adenoid surface is shaped mainly into mucosal folds, not the deep crypt pattern of the palatine tonsil. Both surfaces lie next to lymphoid tissue.
Material passing through the mouth can enter a palatine crypt and meet its lining. Here the amber speck is a harmless bit of food protein that the immune system can recognize as an antigen.
A small sample reaches a local cell
A small sample can reach a dendritic cell near the crypt lining. The close-up shows the idea of sampling, not a single fixed route across the lining.
A dendritic cell meets a T cell
A dendritic cell can display a small fragment of a sampled protein. A nearby T cell can check that display during contact. Sampling does not mean an immune response will follow.
